nodes.label: Order Properties, Sign Rules, and Algebraic Inequalities in ℝ
nodes.explanation: Assumes secondary entry background in real-number arithmetic, rational and irrational numbers as points on the real line, and algebraic manipulation of linear and quadratic expressions, supplying the field properties of ℝ without formal construction. Develops the algebraic order properties of ℝ—trichotomy, transitivity, additive preservation (a < b ⇒ a + c < b + c), and multiplicative sign behavior (multiplying by c > 0 preserves order, while c < 0 reverses it)—together with derived rules for products and quotients (ab > 0 iff a and b share sign; ab < 0 iff they have opposite signs), non-negativity of squares (x² ≥ 0 for all x ∈ ℝ), reciprocal comparison (carefully separating same-sign reversal 0 < a < b ⇒ 1/b < 1/a from opposite-sign preservation a < 0 < b ⇒ 1/a < 1/b), and power monotonicity (a < b ⇔ a³ < b³ on ℝ vs. 0 ≤ a < b ⇔ a² < b² on [0, ∞)). Uses explicit sign-check diagnostics and counterexamples as the key bridge to expose invalid steps—multiplying by an unknown-sign expression, taking reciprocals across zero, or squaring inequalities when one or both sides may be negative. Enables the learner to prove elementary algebraic order implications, derive sharp bounds on composite expressions such as a - b, ab, and 1/a from given variable bounds, and audit algebraic inequality steps for sign errors. Leaves interval notation to a parallel foundation and leaves completeness, least upper bounds, and suprema to Real Analysis.

nodes.label: Intervals, Set-Builder Notation, and Number-Line Operations
nodes.explanation: Assumes secondary entry background in ordering specific real numbers on the number line and reading basic numerical inequalities such as x > 2 or -1 ≤ x < 5. Develops the standard interval representation of connected subsets of ℝ—bounded open (a, b), closed [a, b], and half-open [a, b), (a, b] intervals, unbounded rays (-∞, a), [a, ∞), (-∞, ∞), and degenerate sets ∅ and {a}—together with set-builder notation, number-line diagrams (open vs. solid endpoints), and the set operations of union (∪), intersection (∩), complement (Aᶜ in ℝ), and set difference (A \ B). Emphasizes why ±∞ always receives an open parenthesis, how strict vs. non-strict endpoints behave under complements and intersections (for example, [1, 3)ᶜ = (-∞, 1) ∪ [3, ∞) and (1, 4] ∩ [4, 7) = {4}), and how logical conjunction ('and') corresponds to intersection while disjunction ('or') corresponds to union. Enables the learner to translate fluently among inequalities, set-builder notation, interval notation, and number-line graphs, and to simplify compound unions, intersections, and complements of subsets of ℝ. Leaves algebraic solving of linear and nonlinear inequalities to subsequent lessons.

nodes.label: Linear, Compound, and Parametric Inequalities
nodes.explanation: Synthesizes the order properties of ℝ with interval and set-operation notation to solve single, compound, and parametric linear inequalities cleanly. Develops systematic solution workflows for linear inequalities ax + b ⋚ cx + d, chained double inequalities f(x) < g(x) ≤ h(x) (specifically emphasizing splitting into the conjunction f(x) < g(x) and g(x) ≤ h(x) whenever the variable appears outside the middle expression, rather than performing illegal simultaneous operations), disjunctive 'or' systems, and one-variable linear inequalities containing an unspecified real parameter such as ax + b > c or (m - 2)x ≤ m² - 4. Uses exhaustive case splitting on the sign and vanishing of the variable's coefficient (a > 0, a = 0 yielding ℝ or ∅, and a < 0 reversing the inequality) as the central bridge, directly correcting the common mistake of dividing by a parameter expression without checking zero or sign. Enables the learner to solve arbitrary linear, chained, and parametric linear inequalities and report complete solution sets in simplified interval notation across all parameter regimes. Leaves quadratic and higher-degree inequalities and absolute value inequalities to subsequent lessons.

nodes.label: Quadratic Inequalities and Sign of Quadratic Expressions
nodes.explanation: Synthesizes order properties of ℝ (product sign rules and x² ≥ 0) with interval notation, assuming background from recommended preparation in factoring quadratics, completing the square, and the quadratic formula and discriminant Δ = b² - 4ac. Develops complete algebraic and sign-interval methods for solving ax² + bx + c ⋚ 0 across all three discriminant regimes: Δ > 0 (two distinct real roots partitioning ℝ into three alternating-sign intervals via factored form a(x - r₁)(x - r₂)), Δ = 0 (a repeated root yielding a perfect square a(x - r)² whose solution set may be ℝ, ℝ \ {r}, {r}, or ∅ depending on strictness and sign of a), and Δ < 0 (completing the square to show the quadratic is sign-definite on all of ℝ, producing ℝ or ∅). Connects the algebraic sign analysis to parabola opening direction as a visual cross-check and applies the discriminant-plus-leading-coefficient criterion to solve sign-definiteness parameter problems (such as finding all k for which kx² + 2x + 1 > 0 for every x ∈ ℝ, including checking k = 0). Enables the learner to solve any quadratic inequality accurately including degenerate boundary cases and to characterize always-positive or always-negative quadratics. Leaves higher-degree polynomials and rational inequalities to subsequent lessons.

nodes.label: Higher-Degree Polynomial Inequalities and Sign Charts
nodes.explanation: Builds on quadratic inequalities and sign intervals (and assumes basic polynomial factoring from prior algebra, supplying without proof the continuity fact that a polynomial can change sign only at its real zeros) to establish the critical-point and sign-chart method for factored and factorable polynomial inequalities P(x) ⋚ 0. Develops the multiplicity sign-change rule—a linear factor (x - r)^k changes sign across x = r when k is odd and keeps the same sign when k is even, while irreducible quadratic factors with Δ < 0 preserve constant sign everywhere—and trains building compact factor-by-factor or test-point sign charts. Highlights two decisive pitfalls: dividing both sides by a variable factor such as (x - 2) or (x - 2)² (which drops roots or flips signs), and misclassifying isolated boundary zeros in non-strict inequalities (for example, (x - 2)²(x + 1) ≤ 0 includes the isolated point {2} alongside (-∞, -1], whereas the strict version excludes both). Enables the learner to solve arbitrary factored or factorable polynomial inequalities accurately with complete endpoint accounting. Leaves denominators and domain exclusions to rational inequalities.

nodes.label: Rational Inequalities and Critical-Point Sign Analysis
nodes.explanation: Builds on polynomial sign charts and assumes background from recommended preparation in combining rational expressions over a common denominator and factoring polynomials. Develops the full method for solving rational inequalities R₁(x) ⋚ R₂(x) by moving all terms to one side, combining into a single quotient P(x)/Q(x) ⋚ 0, and recording both numerator zeros and denominator zeros as critical points on a sign chart. Establishes the non-negotiable asymmetry between numerator zeros (included for ≤ and ≥, excluded for < and >) and denominator zeros (always excluded from the domain regardless of strictness), and applies odd/even multiplicity sign rules across both numerator and denominator factors. Directly addresses two pervasive errors: cross-multiplying by an unknown-sign denominator (losing sign flips and changing solution intervals) and canceling a common factor (x - a) from numerator and denominator without preserving the domain exclusion x ≠ a. Enables the learner to solve general rational inequalities cleanly and verify endpoints and undefined points without introducing extraneous boundary points. Leaves absolute values and radicals inside rational expressions to later synthesis lessons.

nodes.label: Absolute Value: Piecewise Definition, Distance, and Basic Inequalities
nodes.explanation: Builds on linear and compound inequalities to develop both the algebraic piecewise definition of |x| and the geometric interpretation of |x - a| as the distance between x and a on the real line. Establishes core algebraic properties—|x| ≥ 0, |-x| = |x|, |xy| = |x||y|, |x/y| = |x|/|y| (y ≠ 0), |x|² = x², and the crucial identity √(x²) = |x| (correcting the frequent error √(x²) = x)—and develops exact equivalences for basic equations and inequalities |A(x)| = c, |A(x)| < c, |A(x)| ≤ c, |A(x)| > c, |A(x)| ≥ c across all signs of the constant c (explicitly handling c ≤ 0 edge cases such as |2x - 1| ≤ 0 or |2x - 1| > -3), two-sided distance bands a < |x - c| ≤ b, and symmetric comparisons |A(x)| = |B(x)| or |A(x)| < |B(x)| (justified by squaring both non-negative sides via A(x)² - B(x)² = (A - B)(A + B)). Enables the learner to translate between distance statements, interval notation, and absolute value inequalities, simplify √(expr²) safely, and solve single- and symmetric two-absolute-value problems. Leaves variable right-hand sides, sums of absolute values, nested cases, and the triangle inequality to the next lessons.

nodes.label: Variable-Bound, Nested, and Sum Absolute Value Inequalities
nodes.explanation: Synthesizes basic absolute value equivalences with quadratic inequalities to solve non-standard absolute value equations and inequalities systematically. Develops four core techniques: (1) variable-bound equivalences—|A(x)| = B(x) ⇔ B(x) ≥ 0 and A(x) = ±B(x), |A(x)| < B(x) ⇔ -B(x) < A(x) < B(x) (explaining why B(x) > 0 is automatically forced), and |A(x)| > B(x) ⇔ A(x) < -B(x) or A(x) > B(x) (explicitly warning why imposing B(x) ≥ 0 erroneously discards valid solutions where B(x) < 0); (2) critical-point interval partitioning for sums and differences of multiple absolute values such as |x - 1| + |2x + 4| ≤ 9 or |x + 2| - |x - 3| > 1, intersecting each branch solution with its defining region and uniting across regions; (3) outside-in peeling or substitution u = |inner| ≥ 0 for nested forms like ||x - 2| - 3| ≤ 1; and (4) quadratic-in-|x| and |quadratic| inequalities such as x² - 3|x| - 4 ≤ 0 and |x² - 2x| < 3. Enables the learner to choose between direct equivalence rules and region splitting on multi-term, nested, and variable-bound absolute value problems without losing negative-bound branches or keeping out-of-region values. Leaves triangle-inequality bounds and radical-absolute hybrids to separate lessons.

nodes.label: The Triangle Inequality, Reverse Triangle Inequality, and Error Bounds
nodes.explanation: Builds on the algebraic and distance properties of absolute value to prove and apply the triangle inequality |a + b| ≤ |a| + |b| and the reverse triangle inequality ||a| - |b|| ≤ |a - b|. Develops two complementary proofs of |a + b| ≤ |a| + |b| (adding -|a| ≤ a ≤ |a| and -|b| ≤ b ≤ |b|, and squaring via |a + b|² = a² + 2ab + b² ≤ (|a| + |b|)²), derives the exact equality condition ab ≥ 0 (same sign or zero), and uses that condition to solve distance-sum equations and inequalities such as |x - 1| + |x - 5| = 4 or |x - 2| + |x + 3| = |2x + 1| directly without lengthy case splitting. Derives ||a| - |b|| ≤ |a - b| via |a| = |(a - b) + b| ≤ |a - b| + |b| and symmetry, and trains practical perturbation and error-bounding skills—given |x - a| < δ, bounding |mx - ma|, |x² - a²| = |x - a||x + a| (using a preliminary bound like δ ≤ 1 to control |x + a|), and |1/x - 1/a| when a ≠ 0. Enables the learner to prove algebraic bounds with the triangle and reverse triangle inequalities, exploit equality cases, and bound perturbed algebraic expressions, preparing for later ε-δ reasoning in calculus without introducing formal limits.

nodes.label: Basic Radical Inequalities: Domain and Sign-Case Splitting
nodes.explanation: Builds on quadratic inequalities and interval set operations, assuming background from recommended preparation in radical manipulation and the principal even-root convention (√u ≥ 0 for u ≥ 0, while ∛u is defined on all of ℝ and preserves sign). Develops exact algebraic equivalences for single- and two-radical inequalities before any squaring occurs: odd-index roots ∛A(x) ⋚ B(x) ⇔ A(x) ⋚ B(x)³ (order-preserving on all of ℝ with no domain restriction); two even roots √A(x) < √B(x) ⇔ 0 ≤ A(x) < B(x); upper-bounded even roots √A(x) < B(x) ⇔ A(x) ≥ 0, B(x) > 0, and A(x) < B(x)² (with the ≤ adjustment B(x) ≥ 0); and lower-bounded even roots √A(x) > B(x) ⇔ (A(x) ≥ 0 ∧ B(x) < 0) ∨ (B(x) ≥ 0 ∧ A(x) > B(x)²). Uses the sign of B(x) as the essential bridge to show why naive squaring both adds extraneous intervals (when A < 0 or B < 0 in √A < B) and deletes valid intervals (when B < 0 in √A > B). Enables the learner to convert single- and paired-radical inequalities into equivalent polynomial systems and solve them completely without sign or domain errors. Leaves multi-radical sums, radical substitutions, and radical-rational quotients to the next lesson.

nodes.label: Multi-Radical, Product, and Quotient Radical Inequalities
nodes.explanation: Synthesizes basic radical inequalities with rational sign-chart analysis to handle inequalities containing multiple radicals or products and quotients of radicals with polynomials. Develops three key strategies: (1) isolating non-negative terms before repeated squaring in sums or differences of radicals such as √(x + 5) - √(x - 1) > 1 or √(2x + 1) + √(x - 3) ≤ 5 (rearranging so both sides are non-negative on the domain before squaring); (2) substitution t = √A(x) ≥ 0 for forms quadratic in a radical (such as x - 3√x + 2 ≤ 0) and multiplying by strictly positive conjugates √A + √B to compare radical differences without altering inequality direction; and (3) domain-guarded sign charts for products and quotients such as √(x - 1)(x² - 4) ≥ 0 or (√(x + 3) - 2)/(x - 5) ≤ 0, highlighting the classic trap that a zero of √(x - 1) at x = 1 satisfies a non-strict product inequality even when the remaining factor is negative, while denominator zeros remain strictly excluded. Enables the learner to select and execute valid algebraic transformations on multi-radical and radical-rational inequalities while preserving exact domains and isolated boundary zeros.

nodes.label: Synthesis: Mixed Rational, Absolute Value, and Radical Inequalities
nodes.explanation: Synthesizes variable-bound and multi-term absolute value inequalities with multi-radical and rational sign analysis to build diagnostic fluency on unfamiliar hybrid inequalities. Works across combined structures—such as rational-absolute inequalities |x - 2|/(x² - 1) ≥ 1, hidden absolute values arising from even-power radicals like √(x² - 4x + 4) < 3 - x (using the established identity √(u²) = |u|), quotients mixing absolute values and radicals like (|x| - 2)/(√(x + 4) - 1) ≤ 0, and inequalities where domain pruning immediately narrows the problem before any algebraic expansion. Trains a disciplined four-step strategic workflow: determine and intersect all domain constraints first, simplify structural identities (√(u²) = |u|, strictly positive factors, sign-definite quadratics), choose the lowest-branching method (sign chart, substitution, case split, or squaring with sign guards), and verify all boundary points and isolated zeros against the original inequality. Enables the learner to analyze and solve unfamiliar precalculus-level hybrid inequalities independently without relying on pre-labeled templates.

nodes.label: Floor and Ceiling Equations and Inequalities
nodes.explanation: Optional enrichment building on linear and compound inequalities to develop equations and inequalities involving the floor (greatest-integer) function ⌊x⌋, ceiling (least-integer) function ⌈x⌉, and fractional part {x} = x - ⌊x⌋ ∈ [0, 1). Establishes the characterizing double inequalities ⌊x⌋ ≤ x < ⌊x⌋ + 1 (so ⌊x⌋ = n ⇔ n ≤ x < n + 1 for n ∈ ℤ) and ⌈x⌉ - 1 < x ≤ ⌈x⌉, and carefully contrasts strict vs. non-strict bounds for integer vs. non-integer constants (for instance, ⌊x⌋ < 3 ⇔ x < 3, whereas ⌊x⌋ < 3.4 ⇔ x < 4, and ⌊x⌋ ≤ 3 ⇔ x < 4). Develops solving linear-inside-floor inequalities such as ⌊2x - 1⌋ ≥ 3, equations coupling x and ⌊x⌋ such as ⌊x⌋ = 2x - 3 or x + ⌊x⌋ < 5 via the integer-plus-fractional-part decomposition x = n + f (n ∈ ℤ, 0 ≤ f < 1) or bounding n = ⌊x⌋ directly. Enables the learner to convert floor and ceiling conditions into exact real intervals and diagnose endpoint mistakes around negative real numbers (such as ⌊-2.3⌋ = -3, not -2).

nodes.label: Classical Algebraic Inequalities: AM-GM and Cauchy-Schwarz
nodes.explanation: Optional enrichment building on quadratic inequalities and sign-definiteness (specifically x² ≥ 0 and the discriminant condition Δ ≤ 0 for an everywhere non-negative quadratic) to develop the elementary AM-GM and Cauchy-Schwarz inequalities. Proves two-variable AM-GM (a + b)/2 ≥ √(ab) for a, b ≥ 0 from (√a - √b)² ≥ 0, extends it to four variables by pairing and to three variables via backward induction (setting the fourth variable to the arithmetic mean of the first three) or the identity x³ + y³ + z³ - 3xyz = (1/2)(x + y + z)[(x - y)² + (y - z)² + (z - x)²] ≥ 0, and proves the finite-sum Cauchy-Schwarz inequality (∑ a_i b_i)² ≤ (∑ a_i²)(∑ b_i²) by viewing P(t) = ∑ (a_i t - b_i)² ≥ 0 as a non-negative quadratic in t whose discriminant cannot be positive. Emphasizes exact equality conditions (a = b for AM-GM; proportionality a_i = λ b_i for Cauchy-Schwarz) and applies both inequalities to prove symmetric algebraic bounds and find exact algebraic minima/maxima (such as x + 4/x for x > 0 or a + 2b subject to a² + b² = 1) without calculus, stressing that a lower bound f(x) ≥ M is only a true minimum once an admissible point achieves equality.
